title: MISO proposes distinct reliability rules for large and computational loads
plain: The Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) has filed a proposal, pending Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approval, that creates separate regulatory classifications for large loads and for a new subcategory called computational loads. angles.claim: Once a 25 megawatt IT threshold sets who faces curtailment, every data center contract signed before FERC rules on it is a bet on terms not yet written.
angles.audience: Directors negotiating data center site and power agreements
angles.rank_reason: Directly changes a decision being made now, since capacity reservations and contract clauses drafted today may not match whatever obligations FERC ultimately approves.

angles.claim: A megawatt threshold drawn to catch data centers will also catch hydrogen plants and battery factories that happen to run dense compute for controls.
angles.audience: Engineers scoping interconnection for industrial and computational loads
angles.rank_reason: Reaches the sector broadly and forces a concrete Monday task, checking whether existing or planned loads cross 25 megawatts of IT equipment, but the consequence is definitional rather than operational until FERC rules.

angles.claim: MISO is building a reliability category with no obligations attached yet, so the filing is a placeholder for rules that will be negotiated after the classification exists.
angles.audience: Regulatory affairs teams tracking FERC proceedings
angles.rank_reason: Ranks last because it restates the article's own stated gap rather than adding a claim the author would need to defend beyond what MISO already disclosed.
